title: Time & Work
summary: Rates, LCM units and the men-days chain solve nearly every question: combined work, efficiency ratios, pipes and cisterns, mid-work join/leave, alternate days, provisions and wages. One slot is near-guaranteed in Tier 1, with staged pipe problems and wage splits rising in Tier 2.

subtopics.title: Work Rates & the LCM Method
subtopics.concept:
Think of a whole job as 1 unit. A person who finishes in T days works at rate $\frac{1}{T}$ per day.

$$\text{combined rate} = \frac{1}{T_1} + \frac{1}{T_2} + \cdots, \qquad T_{\text{together}} = \frac{1}{\text{combined rate}}$$

**LCM method (no fractions):** take total work = LCM of the given days. If A takes 12 and B takes 24, set work = 24 units; A does 2/day, B does 1/day; together 3/day ⇒ 8 days. Whole numbers only — faster and safer.

**Symmetry shortcut:** two workers of times a and b together take $\frac{ab}{a+b}$ days.

tricks.body: Set the job to the LCM of the individual times; rates become small integers.

subtopics.title: Efficiency, 'Twice as Good' & Ratio Cases
subtopics.concept:
Efficiency is rate. **Efficiency is inversely proportional to time**: twice as efficient ⇒ half the days.

$$\frac{\text{efficiency}_A}{\text{efficiency}_B} = \frac{\text{time}_B}{\text{time}_A}$$

If A is k times as good as B and together they take T days: rate $= (k+1)$ units ⇒ B alone takes $(k+1)T$ days, A alone takes $\frac{(k+1)T}{k}$ days.

Convert every 'twice as good / half as efficient' statement into a rate ratio first — everything else is arithmetic.

tricks.title: Rate units from the efficiency ratio
tricks.body: Let B = 1 unit/day, A = k units/day; total = (k+1)/day.

example.q: A is twice as efficient as B, and together they finish a job in 12 days. B alone would take:
example.solution: Units: A + B = 3/day = whole job in 12 ⇒ job = 36 units ⇒ B alone = **36 days** (A: 18).

tricks.title: Invert, never scale
tricks.body: 'A is 3 times as good' ⇒ A's days = B's days ÷ 3.

example.q: A is 3 times as efficient as B and together they complete the work in 12 days. A alone takes:

tricks.title: Days-difference cases
tricks.body: 'B takes 24 days more than A' plus an efficiency ratio pins both times.

example.q: A is 3 times as fast as B and takes 24 days less than B. Together they would finish the work in:
example.solution: Times x and 3x with 3x − x = 24 ⇒ x = 12, so A = 12, B = 36; together $\frac{36}{4} = 9$ days.

mistakes: Scaling days when told efficiency scales ('twice as good' means HALF the days, not double).
Adding efficiencies as days.
Using $kT$ for the stronger worker's time instead of $\frac{(k+1)T}{k}$.
Ignoring that 'x times as fast' and 'x% more efficient' set up different ratios.

subtopics.title: Pipes & Cisterns
subtopics.concept:
Inlets fill (+rate), outlets/leaks drain (−rate). Treat the tank as 1 unit (or LCM litres).

$$\text{net rate} = \sum_{\text{inlets}} \frac{1}{T_i} - \sum_{\text{outlets}} \frac{1}{T_j}, \qquad \text{time} = \frac{1}{\text{net rate}}$$

**Two pipes, one filling one emptying:** net time $= \frac{ab}{b - a}$ (a = fill time, b > a = empty time).

Stage-based problems: compute the work already done in the first stage, then re-solve the remainder with the new set of pipes.

tricks.title: Sign discipline
tricks.body: Empty pipes subtract. Write + and − before adding anything.

example.q: Two pipes fill a tank in 8 hours and 12 hours; a third empties it in 6 hours. With all three open, the tank fills in:

tricks.title: Stage the problem
tricks.body: Finish stage 1 first, then treat the remainder as a fresh tank.

example.q: Pipes A (12 h) and B (16 h) fill a tank. Both run for 4 hours, then a drain (24 h) is also opened. The tank is full after how many more hours?
example.solution: In 4 h: $\frac{7}{48} \times 4 = \frac{7}{12}$ done. New rate $= \frac{7}{48} - \frac{1}{24} = \frac{5}{48}$, so the remainder takes $\frac{5}{12} \div \frac{5}{48} = 4$ h ⇒ total **8 hours**.

tricks.title: Fill-and-drain pair formula
tricks.body: One inlet, one outlet: net time = ab/(b − a).

mistakes: Adding an outlet's rate instead of subtracting it.
Forgetting the tank may already be part-full when a new pipe opens.
Using $\frac{ab}{a+b}$ for a fill-drain pair (that formula is for two inlets).
Reporting the stage-1 time instead of the total time.

subtopics.title: Men–Days–Hours Chain & Provisions
subtopics.concept:
Work is the product of every resource: $\text{Work} = M \times D \times H \times E$ (men, days, hours/day, efficiency).

$$\frac{M_1 D_1 H_1 E_1}{W_1} = \frac{M_2 D_2 H_2 E_2}{W_2}$$

**Same work ⇒ equal products:** $M_1 D_1 = M_2 D_2$. More men ⇒ fewer days (inverse proportion).

**Provisions problems:** stock = men × days. After t days, remaining stock feeds the new headcount: $\text{days} = \frac{M_1 D_{\text{left}}}{M_2}$.

Consumption questions (garrison, fodder, food stores) are men-days problems in disguise.

tricks.title: Multiply resources, equate products
tricks.body: Everything inverse-proportional lands in the numerator; direct-proportional in the denominator.

example.q: 15 men complete a work in 20 days. In how many days will 25 men complete the same work?

tricks.title: Provisions after reinforcement
tricks.body: Stock left = original men × days left; then divide by the new headcount.

example.q: A garrison of 500 men has provisions for 27 days. After 3 days, 300 more men join. The provisions will now last:

tricks.title: Work left after a share is done
tricks.body: First find what fraction remains, then apply men-days to that remainder.

example.q: 45 men start a job they would finish in 16 days. After 4 days, 36 more men join. The remaining work now takes:

mistakes: Putting more men in the numerator of the chain equation (more men ⇒ fewer days ⇒ denominator).
Forgetting to subtract elapsed days in provisions problems.
Counting efficiency twice — E belongs inside the product once.
Applying men-days to the whole work instead of the remaining work.

subtopics.title: Joining / Leaving Mid-work, Alternate Days & Wages
subtopics.concept:
Three classic twists, one method — compute the work actually done by each worker:

- **A leaves after t days:** work done $= \frac{t}{T_A}$; the rest is finished by B alone.
- **Alternate days:** pair the days. A 2-day cycle does $\frac{1}{T_A} + \frac{1}{T_B}$; count complete cycles, then handle the leftover.
- **Wages:** money splits in the ratio of work actually done — i.e. the ratio of daily rates when all work the full time.

Wage ratio for full-time co-workers: $A : B = \frac{1}{T_A} : \frac{1}{T_B} = T_B : T_A$.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Two or three people working together
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Individual completion times given; find the combined time (or reverse).
pyqPatterns.approach: LCM units or ab/(a+b). Three people: rate sum, or abc/(ab+bc+ca).

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Fill pipes + an outlet/leak; find the fill time or who's open when.
pyqPatterns.approach: Net rate with signs; stage the problem when pipes open mid-way.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'A is twice/thrice as efficient', or an efficiency ratio like 3 : 4 is given.
pyqPatterns.approach: Rate ratio first, then units: (k+1) workers' worth of rate = 1/T.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Someone works a few days, then leaves; another (or the group) finishes.
pyqPatterns.approach: Work already done = t/T; apply the remaining fraction to the continuing workers.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A and B work on alternate days (someone starts); find total time or work share.
pyqPatterns.approach: Progress per 2-day cycle; multiply cycles, then finish the tail with whoever's turn it is.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Men, days, hours given in two scenarios (maybe efficiency too) — find the missing one.
pyqPatterns.approach: M₁D₁H₁E₁ = M₂D₂H₂E₂ for the same work; keep inverses in the numerator.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Garrison or hostel stock after reinforcements or early inspection.
pyqPatterns.approach: Stock in man-days: M × D. Subtract elapsed consumption, divide by new headcount.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Total wage for a joint job; find one worker's share.
pyqPatterns.approach: Share = rate × days worked, normalized. Equal days ⇒ rate ratio = wage ratio.

practice.q: A can do $\frac{2}{5}$ of a work in 6 days and B can do $\frac{3}{4}$ of the same work in 9 days. Working together, they complete the work in:
practice.solution:
A: full work in $\frac{6 \times 5}{2} = 15$ days; B: $\frac{9 \times 4}{3} = 12$ days.
Together: $\frac{1}{15} + \frac{1}{12} = \frac{3}{20}$ ⇒ $6\frac{2}{3}$ days.
practice.shortcut: Scale each to full-work time first (15 and 12), then combine.

practice.q: A garrison of 500 men has provisions for 27 days. After 3 days, 300 more men join. The provisions will now last for:
practice.shortcut: 24 days of stock spread over 800 men ⇒ 15 days.

practice.q: A alone completes a work in 12 days and B alone in 18 days. They work together and receive ₹840 as total wages. A's share is:
practice.shortcut: Equal days ⇒ wage ratio = rate ratio = 3 : 2.

practice.q: A can finish a work in 6 days and B in 12 days. They work on alternate days, A starting on the first day. The work is completed in:
practice.solution:
Per 2 days: $\frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{12} = \frac{1}{4}$ of the work.
4 cycles (8 days) complete exactly $4 \times \frac{1}{4} = 1$ ⇒ finished on day 8.

practice.q: 45 men would complete a piece of work in 16 days. They work for 4 days, after which 36 more men join them. The remaining work is now completed in:
practice.solution:
Total work $= 720$ man-days; done in 4 days $= 180$.
Remaining $= 540$ with 81 men ⇒ $\frac{540}{81} = 6\frac{2}{3}$ days.

practice.q: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 12 hours and 16 hours respectively. Both are opened together for 4 hours; then a drain pipe C, which can empty the full tank in 24 hours, is also opened. The total time taken to fill the tank is:
practice.solution:
In 4 h, A + B fill $\frac{7}{48} \times 4 = \frac{7}{12}$; remaining $= \frac{5}{12}$.
New net rate $= \frac{7}{48} - \frac{1}{24} = \frac{5}{48}$ ⇒ time $= \frac{5}{12} \times \frac{48}{5} = 4$ h.
Total = 4 + 4 = **8 hours**.
practice.shortcut: Stage 1 does 7/12; stage 2 rate 5/48 finishes the rest in exactly 4 h.

practice.q: A is 3 times as fast a worker as B and takes 24 days less than B for the same work. If they work together, the work is completed in:
practice.solution:
Times: $x$ and $3x$ with $3x - x = 24$ ⇒ $x = 12$ (A = 12, B = 36).
Together: $\frac{1}{12} + \frac{1}{36} = \frac{4}{36} = \frac{1}{9}$ ⇒ 9 days.
practice.shortcut: Difference of times = 2 units = 24 ⇒ A 12, B 36; ab/(a+b) = 9.
